### **Introduction** 

Movies listed on Letterboxd, a film cataloging and review website, are characterized by a wide range of features and statistics. The metadata associated with a given movie entry, such as genre, theme, language, release year, and cast, may influence how users rate films listed on the site. This project focuses on analyzing the metadata of Letterboxd movie entries in order to identify relationships between those features and user ratings. This is a regression problem, where the target variable is a continuous score range from 0 to 5 (stars). The ML pipeline covers the following components: loading / merging the raw CSV files, preprocessing, feature engineering, exploratory data analysis, base model training, and a stacked ensemble as the final meta-regressor. For our base predictive models, we tested the following techniques: Linear, Ridge, and Lasso Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Decision Trees, and Random Forest. We used the XGBoost Regressor as the ensemble model. The goal is to determine what features of a movie relate to its Letterboxd rating, and to use these relationships to build an enhanced predictive model.

### **Data & Exploratory Data Analysis** 

#### *Dataset*

Source: [https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ky1338/10000-movies-letterboxd-data](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ky1338/10000-movies-letterboxd-data)

The dataset for this project was chosen from Kaggle and consists of ten CSV files covering different features of LetterBoxd’s metadata. In the raw files, there are 22 features across 10 different csv files (Table 1). *movies.csv* contains the core attributes including the target variable (rating), while the remaining files are relational, containing features associated with the movie’s id (*id*). The dataset also has a folder containing movie poster images (stored as .jpgs), which was not used for this project due to time constraints.

### **Decision Trees**

For building the Decision Trees model, using the 481 engineered features, the 80/20 train-test split was stratified on binned rating values, giving us 72,799 training films and 18,200 for evaluation. RMSE, MAE, and R² was tracked throughout.

#### *Baseline Model*

Before tuning anything, we let a fully unconstrained tree grow without any depth limit to establish how badly a single tree can overfit. It reached depth 57 and posted surprisingly decent test metrics  R2 of 0.82, RMSE of 0.17, MAE of 0.08  but this is misleading. A tree that deep has essentially memorized the training data, picking up noise alongside real patterns, and would not hold up reliably on new films. We treated these numbers as a ceiling to beat through proper regularization, not a result to trust.

#### *Depth Sweep / Bias-Variance Tradeoff*

To find the right depth, we swept through nine candidate values while keeping min\_samples\_split=50 and min\_samples\_leaf=20 fixed throughout (Figure 5). Rather than relying on a single test split, we used 3-fold CV RMSE as the decision criterion since it gives a more stable estimate of how the model will generalize. Beyond depth 15, both test and CV RMSE either flatlined or nudged slightly worse, which is a clear sign the tree was starting to chase noise again.

![][image5]Figure 5\. Depth vs RMSE: Bias-Variance Tradeoff

#### *Tuned Model*

The final model combined depth control with a few additional guardrails to subsample features at each split and reduce redundancy between branches and also prune out insignificant branches. On the test set, this produced an R2 of 0.5656, RMSE of 0.2764, and MAE of 0.19. The 5-fold CV RMSE came in at 0.31. In practical terms, 92.1% of predictions landed within half a star of the actual rating, and 72.8% were within a quarter star of reasonable precision given that the entire IQR of the rating distribution spans only about 0.5 stars. The residual mean of 0.0034 is effectively zero, meaning the model is not systematically over- or under-predicting (Figure 6).

![][image6]

Figure 6\. Tuned DT Predicted vs Actual & Residual Distribution

### **Random Forest**

The Random Forest model builds many decision trees on random subsets of the data and features, then averages their predictions. This addresses core weaknesses of using a  
single decision tree such as high variance and sensitivity to noise. Compared to the Random Forest (R2 \= 0.7028, RMSE \= 0.2287), the tuned DT falls short by about 13.7 R2 points. That gap is not surprising — a single tree has to commit to one set of splits, so any instability in the data hits it hard. The Random Forest averages across 100 trees, which smooths out those fluctuations considerably (Figure 7). We kept the Decision Tree in the analysis as a transparent, interpretable reference point, but the Random Forest is the stronger model that we use for the ensemble.

![][image7]  
Figure 7\. Comparing RF with DT

The tuned decision tree explained only 6% of rating variance because it relied entirely on structural signals (description length, taglines, release breadth) with no information about the people who made each film. The three engineered features, *studio\_avg\_rating*, *director\_avg\_rating*, and *actor\_avg\_rating*  account for \~70% of the RF model’s  predictive power (Figure 8). This makes intuitive sense: a film made by a director with a career average of 3.8 star rating is far more likely to rate higher than one whose past films average 2.9 star rating. The remaining unexplained variance (\~28% for RF) is largely driven by features that were not encoded in the metadata. These features shift the approach from "what kind of film is this?" to "who made this film, and what is their track record?" Decision Trees was excluded from the ensemble model stack because RF improved upon DT (i.e RF is an ensemble of DT).

*![][image8]*

Figure 8\. Top 20 Feature Importances: Tuned DT vs Random Forest

### **Linear Regression Models**

#### *Linear Regression*

The Linear Regression model was trained using an 80/20 train-test split. Model performance was evaluated using Mean Squared Error (MSE) and R² score. The model achieved an R² score of approximately 0.867 and an MSE of about 0.023, indicating strong predictive performance and that the model explains a large portion of the variance in movie ratings. A scatter plot of predicted versus actual ratings showed a strong linear trend, confirming that the model effectively captures the relationship between features and ratings.

*![][image9]*  
Figure 9\. Linear Regression Model

#### *Ridge & Lasso Regression*

To further evaluate linear model performance, Ridge and Lasso regression models were tested. Ridge regression achieved a slightly higher R² score of approximately 0.867 with a marginally lower MSE, indicating a small improvement due to coefficient regularization (Table 2). Lasso regression resulted in a slightly lower R² score of approximately 0.855 and a higher MSE, suggesting that removing features reduced model performance. Overall, even though the improvement over basic linear regression was minimal, the ridge regression model demonstrated the strongest predictive capability for estimating movie ratings; the results show that linear models perform effectively on this dataset.

Table 2\. Comparing Regression Models

| Model | RMSE | MAE |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Linear Regression | 0.1526 | 0.1056 |
| Ridge Regression | 0.1526 | 0.1055 |
| Lasso Regression | 0.1594 | 0.1053 |

### **K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)** 

For the fourth model, the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) regression model was used to predict movie ratings. Prior to modeling, a basic analysis was performed to see the distribution of the target variable along with the scales of all the different features. The target variable was found to be mostly normally distributed. With KNN relying on distance calculations, the features were normalized using min-max scaling. MinMax scaling ensures that all features are in the same range and no feature dominates distance calculations.  
   
The initial KNN model was trained using K \= 10\. The model’s performance was evaluated using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), which measures the average deviation between predicted and actual ratings. The baseline model produced a training RMSE of about \~0.264 and a test RMSE of about \~0.29, indicating reasonable performance with minimal overfitting.  
   
To further optimize the model, a sensitivity analysis was done by plotting training and test RMSE for K values from 5 to 100 (in increments of 5). The results showed that small values of K led to overfitting, with low training error but higher test error and large values of K lead to underfitting. The optimal K values are in the 20-30 range, where test RMSE is low and flat, and the gap between training and test RMSE is not too small (Figure 10). Increasing K over this range results in underfitting as the model becomes overly smooth.

![][image10]  
Figure 10\. K Sensitivity Analysis

The final model was trained with K \= 25, and it achieved a test RMSE of \~0.297 (Figure 11). Given that ratings range from 0.9 to 4.7, this equates to an average error of less than 9% of the rating scale. However, it tended to smooth extreme values. The KNN model was somewhat unreliable compared to linear regression and random forest. This model was still chosen to be stacked on the ensemble model in an effort to diversify it.  
![][image11]  
Figure 11\. Fine-tuned KNN Model (k \= 25\)

### **Ensemble Model** 

The final stacked ensemble model was created to combine the predictions from the three chosen models and function as a meta model (meta-regressor). XGBoost Regressor was chosen as the ensemble model. The XGBoost Regressor combines outputs of the three chosen base models (ridge regression, RF, and KNN) to create a more effective predictive model. In the stacking model, out-of-fold predictions were used on the training set to build the meta-regressor. Using 5-fold cross validation, each base model’s predictions were made on data it was never trained on. This prevents data leakage and ensures the ensemble model learns from the predictions. Ridge regression is the most dominant base model; the XGBoost ensemble model barely improves upon it (Table 3). The KNN seems to cumber the ensemble model rather than help it; distance metrics are unreliable for higher dimensions. The XGBoost ensemble only slightly improves upon ridge regression (Figure 12).

Table 3\. Comparison of Stacked Models with Ensemble

| Model | RMSE | MAE | R2 |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Random Forest | 0.2256 | 0.1568 | 0.7092 |
| Ridge Regression | 0.1526 | 0.1055 | 0.8670 |
| KNN (k=25) | 0.2970 | 0.2155 | 0.4957 |
| Ensemble (XGBoost) | 0.1516 | 0.1052 | 0.8687 |

### **Conclusion**

This project proved movie ratings can be accurately predicted with linear regression models, using structural metadata with engineered features. On Letterboxd, who made the movie says more about its rating than what the movie is actually about. Raw data features, such as genre, runtime, language, and country features helped a bit, but they were not driving predictive features. There’s still some variance the model can’t explain, which is expected with the given metadata. Personal taste and cultural context were not accounted for. Plus, the prestige features were calculated strictly from movies released before the target film. Ridge Regression stood out as the strongest base model with the ensemble only offering a small bump; linear models hold their own with well-designed prestige features. 

#### *Future Applications*

The ensemble model can be used to design a personalized movie recommender app that suggests movies for users based on their previous Letterboxd reviews. Movie recommendations can be filtered by genre, theme, cast, director and/or description. Recommendations would be based on both individual user ratings and average ratings, giving users a highly-personalized experience. Utilizing movie poster images from the raw dataset with a convolutional neural network to capture visual features could also add a layer of enhancement to the prediction model (base and ensemble).
